contentHtml:
What GPS fleet tracking means for an Indian business

In short: GPS fleet tracking puts a device in each vehicle that reports its position over a mobile network, so software can show where every vehicle is and what it did. If you run buses, taxis or other public service vehicles, a certified AIS-140 tracker with an emergency button is a legal requirement under rule 125H of the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, and since May 2026 the Supreme Court has told States to stop issuing permits and fitness certificates to vehicles without one. Goods fleets are not covered by that rule, but they use the same devices for trips, idling, fuel and driver reports.

This guide was checked in November 2026. I read the notifications, the court report, the FASTag documents and the vendor price pages on 16 November 2026, and every number below has a link to where it came from.

The better first question is not which tracker to buy, but what you want to know every morning that you do not know today. The device is the same for most fleets. The reports, the rules and the money are not.

Who must fit an AIS-140 tracker: the rule and its dates

The mandate sits in the Central Motor Vehicles Rules, 1989, and it covers public service vehicles, which the Motor Vehicles Act defines. It is not a rule for every commercial vehicle. Here is the chain of notifications as a State transport department quoted them.

The vehicle location tracking mandate, notification by notification

DateNotificationWhat it did
28 November 2016G.S.R. 1095(E), MoRTHInserted rule 125H: tracking device and emergency button mandatory for public service vehicles from 1 April 2018
25 October 2018S.O. 5453(E), MoRTHThe Motor Vehicles (Vehicle Location Tracking Device and Emergency Button) Order, 2018
25 October 2018S.O. 5454(E), MoRTHMandated the device for new public service vehicles registered after 1 January 2019; States set dates for vehicles registered up to 31 December 2018
15 January 2020RT-16011/117018-T, MoRTHStates to check fitment and working status at registration, permit and fitness, in VAHAN
22 February 2021RT-16011/7/2020-T, MoRTHStandard Operating Procedure for device registration and activation in VAHAN

Source: West Bengal Transport Department notification 4267-WT dated 14.11.2022, as published by WBXPress and MoRTH's page for S.O. 5453(E), read 16 November 2026.

Three things in that chain matter for an owner. First, the device has to meet AIS-140 until a matching BIS standard is notified, so a cheap tracker from a marketplace does not count unless it is certified. Second, it is fitted by the vehicle maker, its authorised dealer or the operator, under the same standard. Third, the check happens in VAHAN when you register a vehicle, renew a permit or renew fitness, so the device has to be registered and activated, not just screwed in.

Dates for older vehicles were left to the States, and they differ. West Bengal, for example, gave transport vehicles registered up to 31 December 2018 a window of 1 December 2022 to 31 March 2023, and said permits and fitness certificates would not be renewed without the device. Your State transport department's notification is the one that applies to you, so read it before you plan a budget.

What the Supreme Court said in May 2026

On 13 May 2026 a Bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K.V. Viswanathan directed all States and Union Territories to enforce the rules on speed governors, tracking devices and panic buttons in passenger transport vehicles, according to The Hindu's report. The court said fitness certificates or permits should not be issued to public service vehicles that do not comply.

The figures quoted in court explain why. The amicus curiae said that, according to data placed before Parliament in 2024, speed-limiting devices were installed in less than 5% of transport vehicles and tracking devices in fewer than 1%. The court also told States to retrofit existing vehicles and link compliance data to VAHAN.

In practice: if you run public service vehicles, expect the RTO to look for an active device at your next permit or fitness renewal. If you fitted one years ago and let the SIM lapse, check it is still reporting.

What a tracking system should report

The legal device sends location and emergency alerts to a government backend. That keeps you compliant. It does not tell you anything about your business unless the same data, or a second feed, reaches software you look at. These are the reports I would ask any vendor to show me on a real vehicle before signing.

The reports worth paying for, and the question each one answers

ReportWhat it showsThe question it answers
TripsStart, stops, end, distance and time for each vehicle per dayDid the vehicle do the route it was paid for?
IdlingTime with ignition on and the vehicle not movingWhere is fuel being burnt for nothing?
FuelFuel level or fuel used, if a fuel sensor is fitted, against distanceDo fuel bills match the distance driven?
GeofencesAlerts when a vehicle enters or leaves a marked areaDid the truck reach the warehouse, the school or the customer's gate?
Driver behaviourOver-speeding, harsh braking, harsh acceleration, night drivingWhich drivers need a conversation before an accident?
Device healthLast report time, power cuts, tamper eventsIs the tracker actually working, or has someone pulled the wire?

Source: Fleetx's AIS-140 buyer's guide and The Hindu's report of the May 2026 order, read 16 November 2026.

A GPS tracker does not measure fuel on its own. Fuel reports need a fuel sensor or the vehicle's own data; estimates from distance alone are guesses.

Device health is the report most people forget. Ask for a daily list of vehicles that have not reported in the last few hours, and make someone responsible for it.

What devices and SIMs cost

No government page I read publishes a device price. Vendors do, and the range is wide because a quoted price can mean the bare device, the device with a SIM, or a bundle with software and installation. These are the published figures I found.

Published AIS-140 device and running costs, as shown on 16 November 2026

ItemPublished figureWhere it comes from
AIS-140 tracker, device only₹4,200GeoSafe product page; the page does not say what else is included
Entry AIS-140 tracker with SIM₹5,500 to ₹9,000Fleetx buyer's guide, vendor estimate
Installation₹500 to ₹1,500 one timeFleetx buyer's guide, vendor estimate
SIM or data plan₹150 to ₹350 a monthFleetx buyer's guide, vendor estimate
Fleet tracking software licence₹200 to ₹800 per vehicle a monthFleetx buyer's guide, vendor estimate
State VLTD registration fee₹500 to ₹2,000 one time, varies by StateFleetx buyer's guide, vendor estimate

Source: GeoSafe AIS 140 GPS Tracker and Fleetx, AIS 140 GPS Device Price in India (2026), read 16 November 2026.

Treat the Fleetx figures as one vendor's view, not an official rate. They do show that monthly data and software fees outrun the hardware over three years, so compare quotes on a three-year total per vehicle.

Before you sign, ask to see the AIS-140 certificate, who pays for the SIM after year one, whether the vendor activates the device in VAHAN for your State, and whether you can export your own data if you leave.

FASTag: the second location trail you already have

Every vehicle on a national highway already carries a second tracker of sorts. FASTag is an RFID tag on the windscreen, and according to IHMCL's FASTag page it works at over 750 toll plazas, including all national highway plazas and over 100 State highway plazas. One of the listed benefits for road users is toll statements that can be mailed or seen online.

Under the NETC procedural guidelines, the issuing bank should send an SMS after each toll transaction with the plaza and the toll amount, and only one FASTag is allowed per vehicle. For a fleet that is a cheap second record: each toll crossing is a timestamped point on the route, and the statement is a log you can match against your GPS trips and your driver's toll claims.

There is also an official route to this data for logistics businesses. The government's Unified Logistics Interface Platform, ULIP, offers APIs to registered companies after a review of their use case, and a PIB release from March 2023 described a logistics technology firm using ULIP's FASTag API as a tracking tool wherever there is no GPS device or consent available.

One thing FASTag will not do for a fleet: the annual pass. IHMCL's annual pass FAQ says it is only for private non-commercial cars, jeeps and vans, checked against VAHAN, and that use in a commercial vehicle leads to immediate deactivation.

Build, buy or both

For most fleets under a few hundred vehicles, I would split it like this.

  • Buy the certified device, the SIM, VAHAN activation and the core tracking software. Certification, State backends and device firmware are not where your money should go.
  • Build the link between tracking and your own work: trips matched to orders or school routes, alerts on WhatsApp to the right person, a driver app for proof of delivery, and reports in the format your accountant uses.
  • Own the data. Whatever you buy, ask for an API or a daily export, so your trip history sits in your own database and survives a change of vendor.

Building the platform itself makes sense when tracking is the product. If that is you, our notes on GPS tracking solutions and logistics software describe the kind of work involved.

Step by step: rolling out tracking

This is the order I would follow for a fleet of 10 to 100 vehicles.

Step 1. List your vehicles by category. Mark which ones are public service vehicles under your State's rules and which are goods vehicles. Only the first group needs AIS-140 by law; the second group can use any tracker that gives you the reports you want.

Step 2. Read your State's notification. Find the dates for older vehicles and any list of empanelled device makers.

Step 3. Write down the six reports you want. Use the table above. Decide who reads each one and how often. A report nobody owns is a report nobody acts on.

Step 4. Get three quotes on a three-year total. Device, installation, SIM, software, VAHAN activation and replacement. Ask for the AIS-140 certificate and a sample data export.

Step 5. Pilot on five vehicles for a month. Check the trip report against the driver's log sheet and the FASTag statement for the same days. If the three disagree, find out why before you fit the rest.

Step 6. Tell drivers in writing before the devices go live. What is tracked, when, why, who sees it and how long it is kept. This is good practice now and it lines up with the DPDP rules below.

Step 7. Roll out and set a weekly review. Use the routine at the end of this post.

Driver data and the DPDP Act

A tracker records where a person was, minute by minute. Under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, that is personal data of the driver, and your business is the Data Fiduciary for it.

The Rules were notified in November 2025. The PIB backgrounder gives the date as 14 November 2025 and describes an eighteen-month period for phased compliance; a Legal 500 article puts the date most substantive obligations start at 13 May 2027. The backgrounder lists what you will owe people: a clear notice of the purpose, a contact for questions, a response to access, correction and erasure requests within ninety days, and notice to affected people if there is a breach. It also lists penalties of up to ₹250 crore for failing to keep reasonable security safeguards.

For drivers on your payroll, section 7(i) of the Act lists processing "for the purposes of employment" or to safeguard the employer from loss or liability as a legitimate use, which means consent is not the only basis. That is not a licence to track everything. My reading, and it is a reading, not legal advice:

  • Track the vehicle during duty hours. If drivers take vehicles home, decide what happens to location data off duty and write it down.
  • Collect what the six reports need, not live video of the cabin unless there is a clear reason such as a school bus rule.
  • Keep trip history for a fixed period you can justify, and delete older data on a schedule.
  • Limit who can see live location.

Ask a lawyer to check your notice before May 2027.

Three worked examples

The businesses, fleet sizes and numbers here are illustrative, made up to show the method. They are not real customers. Prices use the published ranges in the cost table above.

A school bus operator

An operator runs 20 buses on contract to two schools. The buses are public service vehicles, so each needs a certified AIS-140 device with an emergency button, registered in VAHAN, or the permits will not be renewed.

The reports that matter are trips and geofences: alerts when a bus leaves the depot, reaches each stop and reaches the school gate. Parents do not need a live map; they need a message when the bus is ten minutes away.

What this tells you: for a bus operator, the legal device is the minimum, and the parent message is what the schools will judge you on. That message is a small piece of software on top of the tracking feed, which is where a build makes sense.

A building material distributor

A distributor runs 12 trucks delivering cement and steel to sites around the city. They are goods vehicles, so AIS-140 is not required by rule 125H, and the owner can choose any tracker.

The owner's problem is diesel. The useful reports are idling time by truck, distance against fuel bills, and a geofence on each site so delivery time is recorded without a phone call. Trucks on national highways also produce FASTag statements, which the accountant can match against toll claims each month.

What this tells you: start from the money question. If fuel is the leak, fit sensors on the worst trucks first and judge the system on the monthly diesel figure.

A cab and tour operator

An operator runs 30 cabs and tempo travellers on permit for corporate pickups and tours. These are public service vehicles, so AIS-140 applies, and the emergency button has to work because passengers rely on it.

The reports that matter are trips matched to bookings for billing, driver behaviour for safety, and device health so a dead tracker does not surface at permit renewal. Drivers here are often contracted, so the written notice and agreement in Step 6 matter more than for staff drivers.

What this tells you: for passenger fleets, compliance and billing come from the same data. If trips are matched to bookings automatically, the trip report becomes the invoice backup, and a driver app for duty slips can remove the paper.

Five ways tracking data misleads you

A parked vehicle and a dead tracker look the same. If the map shows a truck in the yard since yesterday, check the last report time before you believe it.

Idling can be legitimate. A bus cooling while children board is idling for a reason. Look for patterns, not single long stops.

Fuel estimates are not fuel measurements. A report that divides distance by an assumed mileage cannot catch theft. Only a sensor or the vehicle's own data can.

Harsh braking alerts need context. Compare drivers on the same route, not across routes.

Compliance is not visibility. The AIS-140 device sends data to a government backend for emergencies. Unless your vendor also gives you the reports, being compliant tells you nothing about your fleet.

A weekly 30-minute fleet review

Same day each week, same person, with the reports open.

A weekly fleet review, split across 30 minutes

TimeWhat to checkWhat you write down
First 5 minutesDevice health: vehicles that did not report for several hoursWhich trackers to fix, and why they stopped
Next 10 minutesIdling and fuel by vehicle against last weekThe two vehicles to look at more closely
Next 5 minutesDriver behaviour alerts by driver, same routes comparedWho needs a conversation
Next 5 minutesGeofence arrivals against orders or routesMissed or late stops and the reason
Last 5 minutesPermit and fitness renewals due in the next 60 daysWhich devices to check before the RTO visit

Source: The Hindu's report of the May 2026 order and Fleetx's AIS-140 buyer's guide, read 16 November 2026.

If you would rather have the scope and cost of a tracking build written down first, that is what our ₹3,500 requirement analysis produces: a call with the people who would build it, the requirements worked through, and a written fixed quotation and timeline before anything starts (how it works). Code, cloud and credentials stay in your name.

Frequently asked questions

Goods vehicles are not covered by that rule, though some States and contracts may ask for tracking. Check your State transport department's notification for the dates that apply to older vehicles.
